summary: Adds a variance procedure to IETF process rules, an escape for situations where existing procedures are not working or do not seem to apply. It is a Best Current Practice, now historic, and was replaced by RFC 2026.

plainLanguage.summary: An emergency exit in the rules for when they don't fit.

questions: what is the ietf variance procedure
how can ietf bypass its normal procedures
when can the iesg grant a variance
subtitle: An escape clause when IETF procedures hit a deadlock

tldr.problem: Sometimes IETF procedures lead to deadlock or provide no guidance for edge cases, preventing valid standards from advancing.
tldr.mechanism: The IESG can grant a variance to allow a specification to advance on the standards track even if it does not meet all usual requirements, provided the benefits to the Internet community outweigh the costs.
tldr.outcome: This provided a safety valve for exceptional cases. The procedure was later superseded when RFC 1602 was replaced.

today: RFC 1871 is Historic. It was replaced by RFC 2026, which integrated the variance procedure into the main standards process rules.

sections.title: The Problem
sections.content:
The IETF internet standards process, documented in RFC 1602 and RFC 1603, sets clear rules for how specifications move through the standards track. But there are rare situations where following these procedures leads to deadlock, or where the procedures provide no guidance at all. RFC 1871 adds an emergency procedure: a way to break the rules when necessary.

The RFC notes that a major revision of RFC 1602 was underway but would take time. Rather than wait in paralysis, this variance procedure offers an interim fix.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF has strict rules for approving standards. Sometimes those rules cause problems or do not fit a situation. This explains how leaders can make an exception when it is needed.

sections.title: How the Variance Procedure Works
sections.content:
The IESG (Internet Engineering Steering Group) can grant a variance upon the recommendation of the responsible IETF Working Group or ad hoc committee. A variance allows a specification to enter or advance on the standards track even though it does not meet all the requirements of RFC 1602 Section 5.

The procedure has five stages: detecting the problem, proposing a solution, public review through an extended Last Call, accepting the solution and incorporating comments, and finally an appeal process. The IAB (Internet Architecture Board) hears and decides any appeals.
sections.plainLanguage: The process works step by step: someone spots the problem, the IESG proposes an answer, everyone gets a chance to comment, the IESG makes a decision, and the IAB can hear complaints if needed.

sections.title: When Can a Variance Be Granted
sections.content:
The IESG must determine that the likely benefits to the Internet community from advancing the specification outweigh the costs from noncompliance. In making this judgment, the IESG must consider: the technical merit of the specification, whether the standards process goals can be achieved without a variance, what alternatives to granting a variance exist, the collateral and precedential effects of the variance, and the IESG's ability to limit the variance as narrowly as possible.

The IESG also has discretion to limit a variance to particular parts of RFC 1602 Section 5 and to impose additional restrictions as needed to protect the Internet community's interests.
sections.plainLanguage: Before allowing an exception, the IESG must ask: Will this help more than it hurts? Is there a better way? What will this set as an example for the future?

references.text: IAB and IESG, "Internet Standards Process -- Revision 2", RFC 1602, March 1994.
